question: Why do open reasoning language models enter repetitive low-temperature chains of thought, what evidence links looping to imperfect learning, and do hardness-diffused action probabilities, temporally correlated errors, and confidence reinforcement explain when temperature helps or merely masks the problem?

key_findings.claim: Every evaluated reasoning checkpoint exhibits substantial greedy-decoding looping in at least one family, and smaller or distilled models usually loop more than larger relatives or teachers.
key_findings.evidence: On AIME 2024 and 2025, the strict 30-gram/20-repeat detector gives greedy looping fractions 0.76, 0.49, and 0.37 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, and 32B; 0.30 and 0.10 for OpenThinker3 1.5B and 7B versus 0.04 for teacher QwQ-32B; and 0.54 for R1-Distill-Llama-8B. Looping decreases as temperature rises, while smaller students remain longer-winded at high temperature.

key_findings.claim: The capacity, distillation, and difficulty comparisons support an association with learning mismatch but do not identify learning error as the cause of real-model looping.
key_findings.evidence: Checkpoint size, architecture, training data, distillation recipe, RL, token budget, and default top-k/top-p settings vary together, and the actual teacher training distribution or student divergence from it is never measured. Problem difficulty is defined from accuracy at temperature 0.8 and related to looping at temperature 0; Phi-4 reverses the trend because it often solves easy problems before repeating an answer-format phrase.

anchors.section: 2, capacity, hardness, instruct, and RL observations
Appendix A, evaluation details and Phi-4 exception

key_findings.claim: Under a deliberately context-blind learner, maximum likelihood exactly diffuses a hard action's mass across n indistinguishable alternatives while preserving an easy action's probability p.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 1 assumes n equiprobable context classes, target action a_i with mass 1-p in class i, easy action a_0 with mass p, and a learner forced to ignore context. The convex cross-entropy optimization has unique solution q_0=p and q_i=(1-p)/n, so greedy decoding selects the easy action once p exceeds (1-p)/n.

key_findings.claim: The proposition is a clean toy optimization result, but its direct application to free-form language-model actions is heuristic rather than proved.
key_findings.evidence: The language-model discussion treats a variable-length token chunk as an action because token log probabilities add, but it does not construct a normalized mutually exclusive action set, show complete contextual indistinguishability, or account for competing chunk lengths and shared prefixes. The real checkpoints are not shown to satisfy the proposition's context-blind constraint or equiprobable context model.

anchors.section: 3, Formalizing hardness and Mapping to language models

key_findings.claim: A controlled star-graph random walk realizes the hardness mechanism: a learned reset action can outrank every diffused root edge and induce long start-root loops at low temperature.
key_findings.evidence: An approximately 85M-parameter, 12-layer Transformer is trained for 100,000 steps on 2M sequences from modified G(5,5), where forward moves have probability 0.7 and reset has probability 0.3. Low-temperature generations repeatedly alternate between start and root; without off-path exploration, accuracy remains near chance even as temperature shortens loops. With root exploration, accuracy rises with temperature but is near zero greedily.

anchors.section: 3.1-3.2, Markovian intuition, training details, and low-temperature results
3.2, exploration, easier graphs, and reset overestimation

key_findings.claim: Temperature is a partial mitigation rather than a repair in the hardness experiment, and a prominent negative result is that exploration is necessary for accuracy to improve.
key_findings.evidence: At temperature 1, the G(5,5) exploration model averages 105.5 generated tokens versus 24.8 for a perfect learner, more than four times longer. In the no-exploration distribution, increasing temperature reduces loop count but leaves accuracy near chance because all learned restarts revisit the same path distribution.

anchors.section: 3.2-3.3, exploration and Temperature as a mitigation

key_findings.claim: The learned Transformer overestimates the easy reset beyond the teacher's 0.3 probability, strengthening the risk-aversion loop beyond simple mass diffusion.
key_findings.evidence: Across 500 G(5,5)-with-exploration generated trajectories at temperature zero, 94% of root positions assign reset more than 0.3 probability, with mean about 0.35, while the rest is spread roughly uniformly over outgoing root edges. The paper observes a similar pattern on G(5,3) but leaves its source for future work.

key_findings.claim: Even when the training distribution is uniform at the root, learned root-probability errors remain correlated across visits and greedy decoding repeatedly selects the same children.
key_findings.evidence: On the G(5,5) uniform-child task, the top-probability child matches across consecutive root visits 96.7% of the time and the second-ranked child matches 76.7%. A history-dependent margin in the training walk reduces these pairs to 77.1%/53.7% at m=0.05 and 61.6%/48.0% at m=0.1, with lower loops and near-perfect accuracy, but remains far above the perfect margin-aware learner's zero revisit preference.

key_findings.claim: Calling the temporal correlation a Transformer inductive bias is stronger than the controls establish.
key_findings.evidence: The paper reports one decoder-only architecture family and no RNN, Mamba, Markov, alternative positional encoding, different objective, or independently seeded architecture control on the same distribution. Correlation is measured along model-generated trajectories that share histories, so the evidence establishes persistent conditional preferences in these trained Transformers, not a uniquely Transformer-specific or architecture-intrinsic cause.

key_findings.claim: The appendix shows the two mechanisms can combine when the teacher favors the correct root child, but the severity depends on exactly which alternatives the learner can distinguish.
key_findings.evidence: With probability 0.5 on the goal child and 0.5/4 on four wrong children, G(5,5) shows mild looping and near-perfect accuracy. Expanding to G(10,5) while the teacher still visits only five children makes an already visited wrong child retain about 0.125 versus about 0.097 for each indistinguishable alternative, so greedy looping becomes much stronger.

key_findings.claim: Repeated context can reinforce an existing loop, and a 0.001 mixture of deterministic looping traces is sufficient to reproduce this catalyst in the synthetic tasks.
key_findings.evidence: In two selected 30K-token OpenThinker traces, maximum next-token probability rises toward one after the final loop begins. Adding deterministic looping examples with probability 0.001 drives reset or repeated-child probability toward one across successive root visits and increases low-temperature loop counts, response length, and accuracy loss in both hardness and correlated-error variants.

key_findings.claim: The real-trace continuation studies are selected case analyses whose judge and conditioning choices limit causal interpretation.
key_findings.evidence: For two manually selected AIME traces, the authors generate 5 greedy continuations and 50 sampled continuations per model/temperature, then ask GPT-5 whether a hand-listed insight or progress criterion appears. No prompt, judge version, blinded annotation comparison, inter-rater agreement, uncertainty interval, or selection protocol for the two traces is reported; all continuations inherit a student-generated prefix.

key_findings.claim: A disclosed negative case shows that the teacher can share the student's loop, especially after conditioning on an already degraded prefix.
key_findings.evidence: At the second AIME I-5 loop, every one of five QwQ-32B greedy continuations and every student continuation remains in the same enumeration loop. At temperature 0.7, GPT-5 labels progress in only 34/50 teacher and 10/50 student samples; at temperature 1.0, 42/50 versus 27/50. The paper explicitly offers teacher learning error and prefix-induced error accumulation as competing explanations.

key_findings.claim: The looping detector is robust to the tested n-gram thresholds, but it measures exact lexical recurrence and does not cover all semantic cycling discussed by the paper.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 preserves model ordering across (n,k) settings from (20,20) to (40,20), although absolute rates fall for stricter repeat counts. The showcased proof-restart and rechecking loops can be semantic rather than exact 30-gram copies, while instruction checkpoints use k=10 because their outputs are shorter, making their bars not strictly metric-matched to reasoning checkpoints.

key_findings.claim: A reduced GPQA ablation supports domain transfer of the capacity and teacher-student ordering but not the full proposed mechanisms.
key_findings.evidence: On 198 GPQA Diamond questions, four responses per problem at temperatures 0, 0.4, and 0.8 reproduce lower looping for higher-capacity Qwen and OpenThinker checkpoints and for the teacher. The experiment does not test hard/easy splits, inspect actions, measure teacher-student distribution error, or probe temporal correlation on natural traces.

method.core_idea: Triangulate open-model temperature and capacity trends with a minimal graph-generation task in which progress actions, cyclic resets, action indistinguishability, and temporal preference correlations can be controlled and measured.
method.mechanism: A maximum-likelihood lemma predicts that an indistinguishable progress action loses mass to n alternatives while an easy cyclic action retains its mass. Modified star-graph random walks instantiate that imbalance; a second uniform-root task isolates persistent time-correlated preference errors; margin, exploration, graph-size, and rare-loop-mixture interventions vary the resulting loops. Selected real AIME traces and an n-gram detector provide qualitative and aggregate external comparisons.
assumptions: Repeated n-grams are a useful operational proxy for looping, with a different repeat-count threshold for shorter instruction-model outputs.
Within-family size and student-teacher differences are informative about learning mismatch despite unobserved training distributions and co-varying model/training choices.
A logical progress step can be modeled as one action among mutually exclusive chunks, and hard contexts can be approximated by a learner that diffuses probability over indistinguishable actions.

The modified star-graph token process captures relevant atomic features of chain-of-thought even though it omits language semantics, reward training, retrieval, tool use, and accumulated factual state.
Default top-k and top-p settings from each model repository are retained, so temperature is varied within a checkpoint but decoding is not globally standardized across checkpoints.
GPT-5 judgments on selected continuations correctly identify progress-making insights without a reported human calibration study.

techniques.role: Flags a response when an n-gram recurs at least k times and ablates threshold sensitivity.
Measures accuracy, exact looping, and response length from greedy decoding through temperature one.
Uses a constrained maximum-likelihood solution to formalize why indistinguishable hard choices each receive less probability than an easy cyclic action.
Encodes a star graph, start, goal, and random walk as tokens so progress, exploration, reset, and loop events are observable.
Tracks whether the top-ranked root children persist across consecutive visits and relates persistence to repeated paths.
Downweights previously visited root actions in training traces to test whether novelty-biased data reduces learned loops.
Injects deterministic loops into 0.001 of synthetic training traces to test context-conditioned confidence reinforcement.
Compares teacher and student continuations from the same selected prefix using GPT-5 labels for structural insight or progress.

evaluations.setting: AIME 2024 and 2025 across DeepSeek-distilled Qwen/Llama, OpenThinker3/QwQ, Phi-4 reasoning, and instruction counterparts; 20 generations per problem-model-temperature
evaluations.metric: Accuracy, average tokens, and fraction containing a 30-gram repeated at least 20 times for reasoning models
evaluations.result: Greedy looping is common in all reasoning families tested, usually decreases with capacity and temperature, and can be far higher in students than teachers; smaller models remain longer at high temperature.
evaluations.baseline: Within-family model sizes, distilled teacher, instruction checkpoints, and temperatures 0 to 1

evaluations.setting: AIME hard/easy split selected by temperature-0.8 accuracy
evaluations.metric: Temperature-zero looping fraction on the five easiest and five hardest problems per 15-problem split
evaluations.result: Most checkpoints loop more on hard problems, while both Phi-4 reasoning variants loop more on easy problems because of a recurrent post-answer formatting loop.
evaluations.baseline: Hard versus easy selected problem groups; no uncertainty or matched causal intervention

evaluations.setting: GPQA Diamond, 198 questions, Qwen2.5 and OpenThinker3 families, four generations per problem at temperatures 0, 0.4, and 0.8
evaluations.metric: Accuracy, looping fraction, and average chain length
evaluations.result: Capacity and teacher-student looping orderings qualitatively transfer beyond math, with lower looping at higher temperatures.
evaluations.baseline: Model size, teacher versus student, and temperature

evaluations.setting: 85M-parameter Transformer trained on 2M modified G(5,5) or G(5,3) reset-walk sequences
evaluations.metric: Valid goal-reaching accuracy, root-to-start loop count, and response length versus temperature
evaluations.result: Hard G(5,5) yields long low-temperature loops; off-path exploration makes accuracy temperature-sensitive, while easier G(5,3) is near-perfect with brief loops. At temperature one, the exploration learner averages 105.5 tokens versus 24.8 for a perfect learner.
evaluations.baseline: Graph hardness, exploration versus no exploration, perfect learner, and temperature

evaluations.setting: Uniform-root G(5,5) walks and history-dependent margins m=0, 0.05, and 0.1
evaluations.metric: Accuracy, maximum child-visit count, response length, and consecutive-visit top-1/top-2 child agreement over 500 test traces
evaluations.result: At m=0, consecutive top-1/top-2 agreement is 96.7%/76.7%; margins reduce correlation and looping and make accuracy near-perfect, but preferences still recur more than a perfect margin-aware learner.
evaluations.baseline: Margin-free training distribution and ideal root probabilities

evaluations.setting: Combined-hardness root distributions on G(5,5) and G(10,5)
evaluations.metric: Accuracy, maximum child-visit count, and response length versus temperature
evaluations.result: A teacher that puts 0.5 mass on the goal child still induces mild G(5,5) loops; adding indistinguishable unused G(10,5) children makes an already visited wrong child greedily dominant and substantially increases looping.
evaluations.baseline: Five versus ten root children under the same 0.5 correct-action mass

evaluations.setting: Hardness and correlated-error graph tasks with a 0.001 deterministic-loop component in training
evaluations.metric: Action probability by root-visit index, accuracy, loop count, and response length
evaluations.result: The rare component makes loop-action confidence rise toward one across visits and amplifies low-temperature looping and accuracy loss.
evaluations.baseline: Identical synthetic distributions without the rare looping component

evaluations.setting: Two selected OpenThinker3-1.5B AIME prefixes, teacher/student greedy and sampled continuations
evaluations.metric: GPT-5 label for a listed structural insight or valid progress
evaluations.result: Teacher continuations usually progress more often, but at the second loop all five greedy teacher continuations also loop; sampled teacher-student gaps depend strongly on prefix and temperature.
evaluations.baseline: QwQ-32B teacher versus OpenThinker3-1.5B student from the same student-generated prefix

limitations: Author-stated: the graph task is intentionally simple and only isolates a few forces; language-model looping can also involve error accumulation and other mechanisms.

Author-stated: the explanation for Phi-4's inverted hard/easy trend is preliminary, reset overestimation is left unexplained, and the source of increasing confidence during real loops remains future work.
Reviewer-identified: no checkpoint's actual training distribution or divergence from its teacher is measured, so real-model learning error is inferred from associations rather than identified.
Reviewer-identified: size, architecture, data, optimization, distillation, RL, context limits, and decoding defaults co-vary across model comparisons.
Reviewer-identified: top-k and top-p remain model-specific defaults, reasoning and instruction models use different repeat thresholds, and maximum token budgets vary for instruction checkpoints.
Reviewer-identified: exact n-gram recurrence misses semantic proof-restart loops, while the selected examples are not drawn by a preregistered sampling protocol.
Reviewer-identified: reported aggregate plots do not state independent training seeds, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or per-problem dispersion.

Reviewer-identified: the hard/easy analysis selects difficulty using temperature-0.8 accuracy and evaluates temperature-zero loops on the same small problem pool, with Phi-4 providing a clear counterexample to the general trend.
Reviewer-identified: GPT-5 continuation labels lack the exact judge version, prompt, human validation, inter-rater agreement, or uncertainty, and all probes condition on student-generated prefixes.
Reviewer-identified: the temporal-correlation experiment lacks non-Transformer and independently varied architecture/objective controls, so it does not isolate a Transformer-specific inductive bias.

Reviewer-identified: Proposition 1 requires a context-blind learner and mutually exclusive hard actions; its extension to variable-length language chunks is an analogy, not a theorem about the evaluated LMs.
Reviewer-identified: synthetic interventions are not applied to real reasoning-model training, and no real-model mitigation is evaluated beyond changing temperature.
Reviewer-identified: the 0.001 confidence-bias mixture demonstrates sufficiency of a manufactured repeated-trace component, not that such a component caused the real checkpoints' behavior.
Reviewer-identified: the GPQA ablation covers two families with only four samples per question-temperature and tests aggregate transfer, not the proposed action-level mechanisms.
Reviewer-identified: all five teacher continuations loop in one appendix case, directly limiting a simple student-versus-teacher causal account.
failure_modes: If probability on a correct but confusable action is split below an easy reset or restatement action, greedy decoding can enter a stable low-temperature cycle.
Raising temperature can break lexical cycles yet leave accuracy near chance when the training distribution contains no exploratory route to recover the goal.
Persistent small probability skews at a repeated decision point can repeatedly select the same wrong branch even when no single action is hard in the teacher distribution.
Once a repetition appears in the prefix, self-reinforcing conditional confidence can make later escape exponentially less likely in practice.
A long, confused student prefix can induce a stronger teacher to loop, so teacher continuation quality is not an uncontaminated estimate of the teacher's original policy.
Exact n-gram detectors can miss semantically cyclic reasoning that paraphrases its mistakes and can overemphasize literal boilerplate after a correct answer.
Training margins that penalize revisiting may suppress legitimate verification, backtracking, or iterative refinement along with pathological repetition.
Early stopping or high temperature can terminate a loop but also truncate a necessary long proof or introduce invalid exploratory actions.
A mechanism demonstrated on a finite star graph may disappear or reverse when natural language supplies semantic state, external memory, tools, rewards, or variable action length.
Model-family comparisons can falsely attribute a decoding artifact or data-template difference to capacity or distillation error.
reusable_insights: Evaluate repetition with a joint panel of exact-loop rate, semantic-cycle labels, accuracy, and excess response length; any one measure can hide a different failure.
Separate decoding mitigation from distribution repair by comparing high-temperature path length and success to an oracle or teacher, not only whether exact loops disappear.
A cyclic action becomes dangerous when it is both easy to predict and available at a decision point whose progress action is diffuse; controlling either ingredient can break the cycle.
Repeated-decision probability traces reveal temporal error correlation more directly than final-text loop counts.
Training data that gently favors unvisited valid actions can reduce temporal fixation, but should preserve task-necessary revisiting through state-aware rather than blanket penalties.
Rare repeated sequences can dominate conditional behavior after a long matching prefix, so data audits should measure conditional repeat structure rather than only global frequency.
Continuation studies should cross teacher/student prefixes, use blinded human calibration, and report selection rules to distinguish model error from prefix contamination.
open_questions: Does directly estimating teacher-student KL or action-rank error at naturally recurring reasoning states predict looping beyond model size and response length?
Do RNNs, state-space models, and Transformers trained with matched data and objectives exhibit different temporal error correlation on the same graph task?
Which training-time curriculum or architecture change reduces hard-action diffusion on real reasoning traces without requiring a larger model?
Can a semantic loop detector be validated against humans and combined with exact n-grams without relying on a proprietary judge?
How much real reasoning-training data contains reset, reflection, and repeated-span patterns, and does conditional frequency explain confidence buildup quantitatively?
Can state-aware novelty margins reduce loops while retaining beneficial verification and backtracking?
What causal intervention on a fixed checkpoint distinguishes action-distribution error from decoding, prefix contamination, and exposure-bias explanations?
Does temperature still leave a large oracle-normalized length gap after top-k, top-p, repetition penalties, and stop rules are globally matched?

competitive_landscape.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration
competitive_landscape.difference: Holtzman et al. establish that likelihood-maximizing decoding produces bland, repetitive text and propose nucleus sampling. This paper focuses on modern long-chain reasoning, teacher-student capacity gaps, and learning-error mechanisms; temperature plays the exploratory role that nucleus sampling served in the earlier open-ended generation setting.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Text Generation with Unlikelihood Training
competitive_landscape.difference: Welleck et al. argue that likelihood training assigns too much probability to repeats and directly modify the objective with unlikelihood loss. The looping paper instead diagnoses hardness-diffused and time-correlated errors in reasoning models, but tests no comparable training loss on its real checkpoints.

competitive_landscape.title: Relating Neural Text Degeneration to Exposure Bias
competitive_landscape.difference: Chiang and Chen connect mistakes before degeneration, exposure bias, and self-reinforcing amplification in GPT-2. The present paper separates hardness-based risk aversion from temporally correlated action errors in reasoning traces, while its error-accumulation discussion substantially overlaps the earlier exposure-bias account.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning to Break the Loop: Analyzing and Mitigating Repetitions for Neural Text Generation
competitive_landscape.difference: Xu et al. quantify sentence-loop self-reinforcement under greedy decoding and train DITTO on pseudo-repetitions to break it. This paper extends the phenomenon to reasoning models and adds action hardness plus temporal branch correlation, while Appendix E's confidence catalyst closely recapitulates Xu et al.'s earlier self-reinforcement finding.

competitive_landscape.title: Repetition In Repetition Out: Towards Understanding Neural Text Degeneration from the Data Perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. trace degeneration to repeated training text and show attention dropout over repeated words reduces it even with scaling and instruction tuning. This paper hypothesizes that cyclic reasoning actions in training enable loops and injects rare synthetic loops, but it never audits repetition in the evaluated reasoning models' actual data.

competitive_landscape.title: The pitfalls of next-token prediction
competitive_landscape.difference: Bachmann and Nagarajan show next-token training fails on the star-graph planning task and motivate predicting beyond one token. The present paper explicitly builds on that task, adds resets, exploration, temperature, and repeated visits, and turns the predecessor's root-action hardness into one looping mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: The Danger of Overthinking: Examining the Reasoning-Action Dilemma in Agentic Tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: Cuadron et al. measure analysis paralysis, rogue actions, and premature disengagement across 4,018 SWE-bench trajectories and connect overthinking to lower task performance. This paper targets literal and semantic loops under low-temperature chain generation and supplies synthetic learning mechanisms rather than an agent action-timing taxonomy.

competitive_landscape.title: The Evolution of Thought: Tracking LLM Overthinking via Reasoning Dynamics Analysis
competitive_landscape.difference: Wei et al. identify repetitive semantic oscillations and an instance-specific reasoning-completion point on AIME and GPQA, then use termination-token rank dynamics for early exit. This paper asks why exact loops arise and argues for training-time error repair; it does not compare against the already available reasoning-dynamics detector or test an early-exit baseline.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Errors in learning drive low-temperature loops in reasoning models through two mechanisms: hard progress actions lose relative probability to easy cyclic actions, and small Transformer errors remain temporally correlated so the same branches recur; temperature promotes exploration but does not repair either error.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper combines multi-family AIME/GPQA temperature trends, an exact constrained-likelihood proposition, modified star-graph interventions, measured root-action probabilities and cross-visit correlations, margin and graph-size ablations, and rare-loop confidence amplification. Selected AIME continuation probes provide qualitative parallels but do not measure the proposed latent action distributions in real models.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: After comparison with degeneration, exposure-bias, self-reinforcement, repeated-data, star-graph, and reasoning-overthinking work, the strongest novelty is the unified reasoning-model study plus the controlled pairing of action-mass diffusion and temporally persistent branch errors. The basic repetition, confidence reinforcement, training-data, decoding, and star-task ingredients are prior. The paper demonstrates sufficient mechanisms in synthetic Transformers and suggestive correlations in open models; it does not establish that these mechanisms are the dominant causal explanation of real reasoning loops.

reviewer_notes: Complete first-pass reading of all 31 cached pages, including the full open-model protocol, proposition and proof, all synthetic variants, threshold and GPQA ablations, both long trace studies, combined-mechanism appendix, and confidence-bias appendix. The local PDF is visibly arXiv:2512.12895v1; the official arXiv record was checked on 2026-08-23 and still lists only v1 (15 December 2025), while the hashes above pin the exact reviewed bytes. Eight competitor records were checked at their current official arXiv versions. Finding attribution distinguishes author reports, reviewer inference, negative results, and causal overreach. The synthetic mechanism evidence is strong within its narrow task; confidence is lower for transfer to real models because training distributions are unavailable, checkpoints and decoding are not globally matched, selected traces use an uncalibrated GPT-5 judge, and one appendix prefix makes every teacher continuation loop. A second reviewer should verify the raw evaluation code, seeds, prompts, checkpoint revisions, and judge rubric before promotion to verified.
